catalog_quote: The accent in Kongo falls upon the first syllable of the stem. When more than two syllables follow the first syllable, a secondary and weaker accent falls upon the penult. Prefixes do not take the main stress, but if there are two monosyllabic prefixes, the first gets a secondary accent. Sundry disturbing factors tend to interfere with the even application of the above rules.. (Holman Bentley 188…
sweep_summary: Three stress-titled items. (1) Descourvières 1770 'Essay d'une grammaire congo, suivant l'accent Kakongo ou Malemba': 'accent' = the Kakongo/Malemba dialect (Maho H16d), an 18th-century manuscript in the Propaganda Fide museum (Doke 1959); no open copy anywhere searched (archive.org, Gallica SRU, Persée); other variety, low priority. (2) Burssens & van Bulck 1936/37 'Accent in de kongoleesche talen', Kongo-Overzee 3: EBALL tags it tonology; almost certainly about tone in Congo languages generally, coded to Koongo only by area code; Kongo-Overzee vol. 3 is not online (archive.org has only 1950-56; HathiTrust 403); print only, low priority. (3) Laman 1922 'The musical accent or intonation in the Kongo language' (already held by the project, archive.org musicalaccentori00lamarich; flagged as noise but wrongly so): §2 p. 1 and §§28-38 pp. 34-37 are a first-hand stress description of the northern (Kingoyi-area, H16e) dialects — root-syllable accent with penult secondary (agrees with Bentley/catalog default), but strong stress is tone-conditioned (often on the ultima under rising intonation and in level-intonation verbs, on high-pitched prefixes, and mobile in verb inflection), which contradicts the 'strict' qualifier for that variety. Laman 1936 Dictionnaire, Étude phonétique §20 (also held by the project, archive.org dictionnairekikongofrancais; central Mukimbungu dialects) restates the plain rule: principal accent on the root syllable, secondary on the penult, root never atonic — confirms the catalog's classification. Recommendation: keep Bentley 1887:701 as the deciding source for the coded (San Salvador) variety, add Laman 1922 §§2, 28-33 and Laman 1936 §20 to the bibliography with a caution that in Laman's northern dialects strong stress is pitch-driven and not strictly stem-initial; if the catalog entry is meant to cover all of koon1244, the 'strict' flag is contradicted at page grade by Laman 1922. Dom 2018 and Odden 1991 (held by the project from the earlier reading) contain no word-stress statement. all downloads saved and logged in

new_statements.quote: a) The root-accent always falls on the root-syllable. It can be strong or half-strong, stronger or weaker than other syllables of the word, i.e. it can have strong stress or not: baka, to catch; baka, wall; kaba, to divide, to give. [...] Prefixes, as a rule, have no influence on the accent: kiese, joy; kibulu, animal; wabatonda, he loved them. The pitch strongly influences the accent, making it either stronger or weaker. See 28, 29. b) The rhythmic accent is a secondary accent that always falls on the penult. If the final syllable (ultima) gets strong stress, the rhythmic accent is weakened: kangama, to be roasted; sukula, to wash. (p. 1, §2; scanned, diacritics lost)
new_statements.citation: Laman, Karl Edvard (1922). The musical accent or intonation in the Kongo language. Stockholm: Svenska Missionsförbundets Förlag. (northern Kikongo dialects around Kingoyi; Glottolog koon1244)

new_statements.reading: Laman, from phonograms and repeated elicitation, describes a root-anchored dynamic accent: the root (stem-initial) syllable always carries the etymological accent and prefixes are ignored, with a secondary rhythmic accent on the penult — the same shape Bentley 1887:701 gives for San Salvador and the catalog codes as stress placement coded per word length as 10 100 1010 (1 = a stressed syllable). But Laman separates this from the perceptually STRONG stress, which he says is not fixed: it is 'as a rule on the root-vowel, unless the intonation is rising, when it is often on the ultima' (§29a, p. 35), falls on the ultima in level-intonation verbs (§29e), can be equal on root and ultima in trisyllables (§30), can sit on a high-pitched prefix (§29b-c), and shifts with tense/pronominal pitch in verb inflection (§33). For the northern dialects Laman describes, therefore, the default location agrees with the catalog but the 'strict' (exceptionless, weight/tone-blind) coding does not hold; Laman's own 1936 summary for the central Mukimbungu dialects (Étude phonétique §20) restates only the plain root-initial + penult-secondary rule.

new_statements.quote: p. 16: "3. — L'ACCENT TONIQUE. En kikôngo, l'accent tonique se place sur la première syllabe du radical. Exemples : sala, mvula, n'sumuki. Quand le radical a plus de 3 syllabes, un accent tonique secondaire se place sur l'avant-dernière syllabe. Exemples : salasana, zyongololo. L'accent tonique, en règle générale, reste sur la première syllabe du radical, malgré les préfixes et infixes qui peuvent la précéder. Exemples : bakento, zinuni, ita kulusamunina. Parfois, il y a glissement de l'accent tonique du radical verbal vers le préfixe. C'est le cas pour une certaine forme du futur et du subjonctif. Exemple : yâsala." p. 6: "le kikôngo offre la grande facilité de ne pas être une langue tonale, du moins dans ses dialectes principaux, ceux de l'Est."
new_statements.translation: p. 16: "3. The tonic accent. In Kikongo the tonic accent falls on the first syllable of the radical. Examples: sala, mvula, n'sumuki. When the radical has more than 3 syllables, a secondary tonic accent falls on the penultimate syllable. Examples: salasana, zyongololo. As a general rule the tonic accent stays on the first syllable of the radical, in spite of the prefixes and infixes that may precede it. Examples: bakento, zinuni, ita kulusamunina. Sometimes the tonic accent slides from the verbal radical onto the prefix. This is the case for a certain form of the future and of the subjunctive. Example: yâsala." p. 6: "Kikongo offers the great convenience of not being a tone language, at least in its main dialects, those of the East."

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (StressTyp2 stress placement coded per word length as 10 100 1010 10010 (1 = a stressed syllable) = stem-initial primary, penult secondary from four syllables up: Déreau's 3-syllable radicals get no secondary, 4-syllable salasana/zyongololo = 1010) and as Laman 1936 Étude phonétique §20 and Bentley 1887 in existing_statements. Adds: the domain is the radical (prefixes and infixes skipped), the secondary-penult rule is conditioned on radical length > 3 syllables, morphological exceptions (accent shifts to the tense prefix/infix a in the remote future and subjunctive; bakidi pair), and an explicit statement that these eastern/central dialects are not tonal…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress (accent tonique) on the first syllable of the radical (stem), ignoring noun-class prefixes and pronominal prefixes/infixes; when the radical has more than three syllables a secondary stress falls on the penult. The author states the dialects described (Kimanyanga north and south) are not tonal: Laman's tone system 'n'est certainement pas actuellement en vigueur dans les dialectes que nous étudions' (p. 7), pitch being a word-length-dependent intonation contour only (pp. 7-8), while vowel length (marked with the circumflex) is contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Explicit: 'Quand le radical a plus de 3 syllabes, un accent tonique secondaire se place sur l'avant-dernière syllabe' (p. 16; ex. salasana, zyongololo).
new_statements.exceptions: (a) Stress shifts from the radical onto the prefix/infix a in the remote future ('il y a un glissement de l'accent tonique vers la première syllabe de la forme verbale', p. 163, ex. yásala) and in the subjunctive ('un glissement de l'accent tonique vers l'infixe a', p. 132, ex. kásumuka 'qu'il pèche' vs kasumuka 'il a péché'); (b) minimal pair by accent place: bakidi 'ils sont encore' (accent on ki) vs bakidi past of baka (accent on ba) (PDF p. 97 L); (c) after the MU-derived nasal prefix N'/M' one gives 'un fort accent tonique à la première syllabe du radical', whereas with the NI nasal infixed 'on diminuera la vigueur de l'accent tonique et on prolongera le préfixe' (p. 12).
new_statements.identity_note: Déreau describes 'les dialectes du centre du vicariat de Matadi, donc du kimanyanga-nord et du kimanyanga-sud' (p. 6; written at Ngombe-Matadi, 1953), i.e. central Kikongo / Kimanyanga, the dialects he says underlie Laman's dictionary and are closest to San Salvador; western and eastern dialects of the vicariate and Kisundi are excluded. His non-tonal claim is restricted to 'ses dialectes principaux, ceux de l'Est'; he attributes Laman's tone system to dialects such as Kiyombe (yomb1244, a different Glottolog language).

sources.quote: 20. En Kongo, les mots ont, dans la règle, l'accent principal (étymologique) sur la syllabe radicale et un accent secondaire (rythmique) assez fort sur la pénultième. L'intensité mélodique peut affaiblir plus ou moins l'accent étymologique sur la syllabe radicale, mais celle-ci ne peut jamais devenir atone. [Translation: In Kongo, words as a rule have the principal (etymological) accent on the root syllable and a fairly strong secondary (rhythmic) accent on the penult. Melodic intensity can weaken the etymological accent on the root syllable to a greater or lesser degree, but that syllable can never become unstressed.]
sources.locator: Étude phonétique §20 (archive.org scan leaf 12; the scanned carries no printed page number; located via archive.org full-text search, file)
sources.note: Étude phonétique §20 gives the plain rule for Kongo (central dialects around Mukimbungu, per the introduction): principal (etymological) accent on the root syllable, a fairly strong secondary (rhythmic) accent on the penult; melodic intensity (tone) can weaken the root accent but the root syllable can never become unstressed. This is the same stem-initial + penult-secondary pattern as Bentley 1887:701 and the catalog rule; §19 adds that high-toned, long, rising/falling and higher-than-preceding final syllables are more intense, and that this 'intensité mélodique' must not be confused with str…
